disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one full manic episode, often alternating with major depressive episodes, in which mood disturbance is sufficiently severe to cause marked impairment or require hospitalization. Psychotic features such as delusions or hallucinations occur during mood episodes and are typically congruent with the prevailing mood state, though they can also be mood-incongruent. The course is usually recurrent and episodic, with inter-episode recovery that may be incomplete in some individuals, and onset commonly occurs in late adolescence to early adulthood but can emerge later in life. It is distinguished from schizoaffective and primary psychotic disorders by the temporal relationship between psychosis and mood episodes, and from Bipolar II Disorder by the presence of at least one manic (not just hypomanic) episode.

narrative.personality: Hailey is a high-energy, detail-oriented server who is curious and independent, finding balance between intense restaurant work and solitary outdoor and creative pursuits.
narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to her episode, Hailey picked up extra shifts at a new, high-end restaurant that was short-staffed, pushing herself to prove she could handle the busiest sections and mentor newer servers. The combination of long, irregular hours, chronic sleep disruption, and constant sensory overload in the dining room slowly eroded the balance she had maintained through hiking, yoga, and quiet time alone. She began pouring her curiosity into elaborate ideas about restructuring the restaurant and obsessively reading about food safety scandals, feeling increasingly convinced that only she really understood what was happening in the kitchen. As her thinking became more disorganized and her behavior more erratic and intrusive at work, she frightened coworkers with strange comments and eventually was sent home mid-shift; after several nights of bizarre experiences alone in her apartment and an episode in which she left work abruptly insisting she was in danger, her manager and a friend accompanied her to the emergency department, leading to psychiatric admission.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep seeing and hearing things that I know aren’t really there, and it’s starting to scare me.”

narrative.personality: Samantha is warm, sociable, and ambitious, with a creative streak and a tendency toward disorganization and worry when juggling many responsibilities.
narrative.stressor: Samantha and her spouse had been arguing for months about finances, fertility decisions, and how much time she devoted to the restaurant versus home, all while she was trying to position herself for a promotion to shift manager. She threw herself into extra responsibilities at work and community activities—gardening projects, improv rehearsals, and helping friends—partly to avoid the tension at home, stretching her time and emotional reserves thin. After a particularly intense period of feeling unusually driven and confident about opening her own café, she crashed into a prolonged emotional low when a major fight with her spouse ended with talk of a trial separation. Over several weeks she withdrew from line dancing, theater, and even her beloved garden, started calling out sick from shifts, and finally went to her primary care clinic in tears saying she no longer cared about anything she used to love, prompting a referral to psychiatry when her mood changes and recent history suggested a bipolar spectrum illness.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I don’t enjoy any of the things I used to love doing anymore, and I just can’t seem to care about them.”

narrative.personality: Elizabeth is a creative, socially engaged former quality-control professional who mixes analytical rigor with spontaneous, artsy energy and a fondness for starting new projects on a whim.
narrative.stressor: After retiring from her long-term quality control role, Elizabeth initially felt exhilarated by the freedom to hike, paint, and design workshops for other seniors, but she also struggled with the loss of structure and professional identity that had anchored her for decades. She began filling her days with increasingly ambitious plans—launching a ‘Quality Champion’ program, organizing multiple art groups, and volunteering at the senior center—sleeping less and talking endlessly about her ideas to anyone who would listen. Friends and family noticed that her once quirky but focused enthusiasm had escalated into nonstop, tangential monologues and impulsive commitments she could not keep, and she grew irritable when others suggested she slow down. When her speech became so rapid and pressured in a senior center meeting that others could not interrupt her, and she began making grandiose, implausible claims about her influence in the local arts community, her adult daughter brought her to a psychiatrist out of concern that this went far beyond her usual energetic personality.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to slow down when I’m talking—my thoughts and words just keep coming out too fast.”
